topics.subject: life
topics.title: Mitosis & the cell cycle

notes.heading: What happens before mitosis?
notes.body: During interphase the cell grows and, in S phase, replicates DNA. Each duplicated chromosome has two sister chromatids before division. DNA replication is essential for equal genetic information.

notes.heading: What is the PMAT sequence?
notes.body: Prophase: chromosomes condense. Metaphase: chromosomes line up at the equator. Anaphase: sister chromatids separate to opposite poles. Telophase: nuclei reform; cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.

notes.heading: What is the outcome of mitosis?
notes.body: In normal mitosis, two daughter cells keep the parent cell’s chromosome number and are genetically identical, apart from possible mutations. Mitosis supports growth, repair and asexual reproduction.

practice.question: A body cell with 6 chromosomes divides by normal mitosis. How many daughter cells form and how many chromosomes are in each?
practice.answer: Two daughter cells form. Each has 6 chromosomes, the same chromosome number as the parent cell.

practice.question: Distinguish metaphase from anaphase.
practice.answer: At metaphase, duplicated chromosomes align at the equator. At anaphase, sister chromatids separate at the centromeres and move to opposite poles.

practice.question: A cell is observed with condensed chromosomes arranged at the equator. Identify the mitotic phase and the next main event.
practice.answer: This is metaphase. In the next phase, anaphase, sister chromatids separate at their centromeres and move toward opposite poles.

practice.question: Why must DNA replicate before normal mitosis?
practice.answer: Replication creates two copies of each chromosome’s genetic information. When sister chromatids separate, each daughter nucleus can receive a complete, equivalent set.

practice.question: A body cell with 8 chromosomes undergoes two successive rounds of normal mitosis. How many cells result, and how many chromosomes are in each?
practice.answer: The first division makes 2 cells; each divides again to make 4 cells in total. Each daughter cell retains 8 chromosomes, assuming normal division and no chromosome loss.

practice.question: Distinguish mitosis from cytokinesis.
practice.answer: Mitosis divides replicated nuclear genetic material into daughter nuclei. Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm and separates the cell into two daughter cells; the processes are connected but distinct.

topics.tip: Do not confuse DNA replication in interphase with chromosome separation in anaphase. The supplied 2022 memo has an inconsistent stage description.

challenges.question: A normal diploid cell has 4 chromosomes before DNA replication. State its chromosome and chromatid counts at metaphase, then the chromosome count in each daughter cell after normal mitosis. Explain the counting convention.
challenges.answer: After replication, metaphase still has 4 chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids, so there are 8 chromatids. Chromosome number is counted by centromeres, not by DNA copies. When division is completed normally, each daughter cell has 4 chromosomes. Replication doubles DNA content without doubling metaphase chromosome number.

challenges.question: In a cell with 6 duplicated chromosomes, one pair of sister chromatids fails to separate while the others segregate normally. Predict the daughter-cell chromosome numbers and explain why normal mitosis is important for tissue repair.
challenges.answer: The affected chromosome’s two chromatids go to one daughter instead of one to each. With all other segregation normal, the daughters receive 7 and 5 chromosomes rather than 6 each. Normal mitosis preserves the full chromosome complement during growth and repair; unequal segregation can disrupt cell function. The numbers assume the single stated segregation error.

cards.front: What happens before mitosis?
cards.back: During interphase the cell grows and, in S phase, replicates DNA. Each duplicated chromosome has two sister chromatids before division. DNA replication is essential for equal genetic information.

cards.front: What is the PMAT sequence?
cards.back: Prophase: chromosomes condense. Metaphase: chromosomes line up at the equator. Anaphase: sister chromatids separate to opposite poles. Telophase: nuclei reform; cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.

cards.front: What is the outcome of mitosis?
cards.back: In normal mitosis, two daughter cells keep the parent cell’s chromosome number and are genetically identical, apart from possible mutations. Mitosis supports growth, repair and asexual reproduction.

cards.front: A body cell with 6 chromosomes divides by normal mitosis. How many daughter cells form and how many chromosomes are in each?
cards.back: Two daughter cells form. Each has 6 chromosomes, the same chromosome number as the parent cell.

cards.front: Distinguish metaphase from anaphase.
cards.back: At metaphase, duplicated chromosomes align at the equator. At anaphase, sister chromatids separate at the centromeres and move to opposite poles.

cards.front: A cell is observed with condensed chromosomes arranged at the equator. Identify the mitotic phase and the next main event.
cards.back: This is metaphase. In the next phase, anaphase, sister chromatids separate at their centromeres and move toward opposite poles.

cards.front: Why must DNA replicate before normal mitosis?
cards.back: Replication creates two copies of each chromosome’s genetic information. When sister chromatids separate, each daughter nucleus can receive a complete, equivalent set.

cards.front: A body cell with 8 chromosomes undergoes two successive rounds of normal mitosis. How many cells result, and how many chromosomes are in each?

cards.front: Distinguish mitosis from cytokinesis.
cards.back: Mitosis divides replicated nuclear genetic material into daughter nuclei. Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm and separates the cell into two daughter cells; the processes are connected but distinct.

cards.front: At which stage are sister chromatids normally separated?
cards.back: Anaphase.

cards.front: Does DNA replication occur during mitosis?
cards.back: It occurs before mitosis, in the S phase of interphase.

cards.front: What distinguishes a chromosome count from a chromatid count at metaphase?
cards.back: A duplicated chromosome has one joined centromere region but two sister chromatids.

cards.front: What is cytokinesis?

topics.subject: life
topics.title: Enzymes & biological molecules

notes.heading: How does an enzyme act?
notes.body: An enzyme is a biological catalyst. Its active site binds a suitable substrate, helping a reaction proceed with a lower activation energy. Products leave and the enzyme can be reused.

notes.heading: Why do temperature and pH matter?
notes.body: Activity usually increases with temperature up to an optimum. Excess heat or unsuitable pH can alter the active-site shape. Denaturation reduces binding and activity; cooling is not the same as denaturing.

notes.heading: What happens as substrate increases?
notes.body: At fixed enzyme concentration the reaction rate rises, then levels off as active sites become saturated. More substrate cannot increase the maximum rate unless more active enzyme is available.

practice.question: Why can a high temperature reduce the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction?
practice.answer: Heat can disrupt bonds maintaining enzyme shape. The active site changes, so fewer substrates bind and fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form.

practice.question: An enzyme reaction stops getting faster when more substrate is added. Explain.
practice.answer: The available active sites are occupied: the enzymes are saturated. Enzyme concentration is now limiting, so adding substrate alone does not raise the maximum rate.

practice.question: Explain why lactase acts on lactose but not on every other food molecule.
practice.answer: The shape and chemical properties of lactase’s active site allow suitable interaction with lactose. Other molecules may not bind correctly, so enzyme specificity limits which reactions it catalyses.

practice.question: An enzyme reaction runs slowly at 5°C but speeds up after warming to its optimum. Does the initial slow rate prove denaturation?
practice.answer: No. Low temperature usually reduces particle movement and successful encounters, slowing the reaction. Recovery after warming is consistent with the enzyme retaining its functional shape.

practice.question: An enzyme concentration is doubled while substrate remains plentiful and other conditions stay optimal. Predict the initial effect on reaction rate.
practice.answer: More enzyme supplies more available active sites, so more substrate can be processed at once and the initial rate should increase. The exact increase depends on the experimental conditions.

practice.question: Name a test for starch and state a positive result.
practice.answer: Add iodine solution to the sample under appropriate laboratory instructions. A blue-black colour indicates starch; iodine solution remaining yellow-brown is a negative result.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: With fixed enzyme concentration, initial reaction rates at increasing substrate concentrations are 2, 4, 7, 8 and 8 units/min. Explain the plateau and predict the effect of adding more active enzyme to the final mixture, assuming substrate remains plentiful.
challenges.answer: At high substrate concentration, nearly all available active sites are occupied, so enzyme concentration limits the rate. More substrate alone gives little increase. Adding active enzyme provides additional active sites and should increase the maximum attainable rate if other conditions and substrate supply remain suitable. The data do not show that the enzyme was consumed.

challenges.question: Two enzyme samples are treated differently: A is cooled to 5°C and B heated to 90°C. Both are later returned to the same optimum temperature and tested identically. A recovers its activity but B does not. Explain and propose one controlled variable needed for the comparison.
challenges.answer: Cooling can slow molecular movement without permanently disrupting the enzyme, so A can recover after warming. High heat can denature B, altering the active site so normal binding does not return. Keep pH, enzyme amount, substrate concentration and testing time equivalent. A comparison should also check that both samples underwent the same final assay conditions.

topics.subject: life
topics.title: Digestion & blood-glucose control

notes.heading: What are digestion and absorption?
notes.body: Digestion breaks large food molecules into smaller soluble molecules. Absorption moves these molecules across the intestinal wall into blood or lymph. Most nutrient absorption occurs in the small intestine.

notes.heading: What does bile do?
notes.body: The liver produces bile; the gall bladder stores and concentrates it. Bile emulsifies fats into droplets, increasing surface area for lipase. Emulsification is physical and bile is not a digestive enzyme.

notes.heading: How is blood glucose regulated?
notes.body: High glucose stimulates pancreatic insulin release, increasing glucose uptake and glycogen formation. Low glucose stimulates glucagon, promoting liver glycogen breakdown and glucose release. This is negative feedback.

topics.formula: High glucose → insulin  •  Low glucose → glucagon

practice.question: Explain how villi improve absorption.
practice.answer: Villi and microvilli increase surface area. A thin epithelium shortens diffusion distance. Blood capillaries and lacteals carry absorbed nutrients away, helping maintain transport gradients.

practice.question: Describe the response to a rise in blood glucose after a meal.
practice.answer: Pancreatic beta cells release insulin. Body cells increase glucose uptake and the liver and muscles store glucose as glycogen. Blood glucose falls toward its regulated range.

practice.question: Distinguish mechanical digestion from chemical digestion and give one example of each.
practice.answer: Mechanical digestion physically breaks food into smaller pieces, such as chewing. Chemical digestion breaks chemical bonds in large molecules, for example amylase acting on starch.

practice.question: Explain why emulsifying fats increases the effectiveness of lipase.
practice.answer: Emulsification breaks large fat globules into smaller droplets, increasing total surface area. More fat surface is available for lipase action. Bile itself is not the fat-digesting enzyme.

practice.question: Blood glucose falls between meals. Name the main pancreatic hormone involved in raising it and describe its effect on the liver.
practice.answer: Glucagon is released. It promotes breakdown of liver glycogen and release of glucose into the blood, helping return blood glucose toward its regulated range.

practice.question: Why does the small intestine have both a large surface area and a good blood supply?
practice.answer: Villi and microvilli provide a large area for absorption. Blood carries many absorbed nutrients away and helps maintain concentration gradients, supporting continued uptake.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: A diagram claims bile chemically digests fats and the small intestine mainly stores the absorbed glucose. Correct both statements and trace how absorbed glucose can be stored after a meal.
challenges.answer: Bile emulsifies fat physically, producing small droplets that provide more surface for lipase; it is not the enzyme chemically hydrolysing fat. The small intestine is a major site of nutrient absorption. Absorbed glucose enters blood and can be taken up by tissues; insulin promotes storage as glycogen in the liver and muscles when glucose is high.

challenges.question: A meal raises blood glucose, followed later by a return toward its regulated range. Describe the negative-feedback response. Then explain why the graph alone cannot establish that the person has normal insulin sensitivity.
challenges.answer: The rise stimulates pancreatic insulin release. Insulin supports glucose uptake and glycogen formation, tending to lower blood glucose and reduce the original stimulus. A glucose graph alone does not measure insulin levels, sensitivity or other influences such as meal size, exercise and timing. Multiple mechanisms can produce similar curves, so a clinical conclusion would require more evidence.

topics.subject: life
topics.title: Photosynthesis & cellular respiration

notes.heading: What does photosynthesis achieve?
notes.body: In chloroplasts, light energy supports the conversion of carbon dioxide and water into organic molecules, with oxygen released. Chlorophyll absorbs light. Plants build biomass from the products.

notes.heading: What does respiration achieve?
notes.body: Cellular respiration transfers energy from organic molecules to ATP. Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm; most aerobic ATP production involves mitochondria. Plants respire as well as photosynthesise.

notes.heading: How are the processes connected?
notes.body: Photosynthesis stores energy in organic molecules; respiration makes that energy available for cell work. Matter cycles between organisms and the environment, but energy flows and is eventually dissipated as heat.

practice.question: Name the reactants and products in the simplified photosynthesis equation.
practice.answer: Reactants are carbon dioxide and water, using light energy. Products are glucose and oxygen.

practice.question: Do plants respire at night? Explain.
practice.answer: Yes. Living plant cells require ATP continuously, so respiration continues day and night. Photosynthesis depends on light and does not proceed normally in darkness.

practice.question: Explain why a plant may show no net carbon-dioxide exchange at a particular light intensity.
practice.answer: At the compensation point, carbon dioxide uptake by photosynthesis equals carbon dioxide release by respiration. Both processes continue, but their opposing rates balance, giving no net exchange.

practice.question: Name the pigment that absorbs light for photosynthesis and the organelle containing it.
practice.answer: The pigment is chlorophyll, located in the thylakoid membranes within chloroplasts.

practice.question: State the reactants and main products of aerobic cellular respiration in a simplified equation.
practice.answer: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, with energy transferred to ATP and released as heat. A balanced summary is C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O.

practice.question: A green plant is kept in darkness. Which continues: respiration, photosynthesis, both or neither? Explain.
practice.answer: Respiration continues in living cells to supply ATP. Photosynthesis cannot proceed normally without light energy, so the two processes do not both continue normally in darkness.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: A plant releases 3 units of CO₂ per hour in darkness. At moderate light it takes up a net 5 units per hour. Assuming respiration remains 3 units per hour, calculate gross CO₂ uptake by photosynthesis and explain a limitation of that assumption.
challenges.answer: Net uptake = gross photosynthetic uptake − respiratory release. Thus 5 = gross − 3, so gross uptake = 8 units/hour. This calculation assumes the respiratory rate is unchanged between darkness and light; real rates can vary with temperature, physiology and other conditions.

challenges.question: An illuminated plant is given labelled carbon dioxide and later the label appears in its sugars. Explain the inference, then describe how some labelled carbon might return to the air and why energy is not recycled in the same way.
challenges.answer: The label supports the incorporation of carbon from CO₂ into organic molecules during photosynthesis. Later respiration can break down those molecules and release labelled CO₂. Carbon atoms can cycle through organisms and the environment. Energy enters mainly as light, is transferred through chemical processes and is eventually dissipated as heat rather than cycling back as the same usable sunlight.

topics.subject: life
topics.title: Plant transport & adaptations

notes.heading: What do xylem and phloem transport?
notes.body: Xylem carries water and mineral ions mainly from roots toward leaves through mostly dead conducting cells. Phloem translocates dissolved organic substances between sources and sinks through living tissue.

notes.heading: How do stomata open?
notes.body: Guard cells take up solutes, lowering their water potential. Water enters by osmosis and guard cells become turgid, opening the pore. Water loss makes them flaccid and closes it.

notes.heading: How do leaves limit water loss?
notes.body: A thick waxy cuticle, reduced leaf area, hairs or sunken stomata can reduce water loss. Explain how a named feature works in the environment; a feature is not useful in every habitat.

topics.formula: Water enters guard cells → turgor increases → pore opens

practice.question: Give two differences between xylem and phloem.
practice.answer: Xylem transports water/mineral ions and its main conducting cells are dead at maturity. Phloem transports sugars/other organic solutes and its conducting tissue is living.

practice.question: Explain why a waxy cuticle benefits a plant in a dry habitat.
practice.answer: The waxy layer limits evaporation from the leaf surface. This reduces water loss when water is scarce and helps the plant maintain cell turgor.

practice.question: Explain how root hairs help a plant absorb water and mineral ions.
practice.answer: Root hairs greatly increase the surface area in contact with soil water. Water can enter by osmosis when water potential favours entry, while ions cross membranes by appropriate transport processes, including active transport.

practice.question: Guard cells lose water. Predict the effect on the stomatal pore and water loss.
practice.answer: The guard cells become less turgid and the pore tends to close. This reduces transpiration through the stomata, although it also limits gas exchange.

practice.question: Give two leaf features that can reduce water loss in a dry habitat and explain each.
practice.answer: A thick waxy cuticle limits evaporation from the surface. Reduced leaf area decreases the surface exposed for water loss. Other justified features include hairs or sunken stomata that maintain a humid boundary layer.

practice.question: Why can phloem transport be described in terms of sources and sinks rather than simply upward movement?
practice.answer: A source supplies organic solutes, for example a photosynthesising leaf. A sink uses or stores them, for example a growing root or fruit. Sources and sinks occur in different positions, so transport is not described by one fixed upward direction.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: A plant is moved from humid still air to dry moving air, while light and temperature initially remain constant. Predict the initial effect on transpiration, then explain how stomatal closure could alter that prediction later.
challenges.answer: Dry air increases the water-vapour gradient and moving air removes the humid boundary layer, so transpiration can initially increase if stomata remain open. Later water stress may reduce guard-cell turgor and close stomata, decreasing loss. Thus the longer-term result depends on the plant’s physiological response, not only the initial environmental change.

challenges.question: A ring of bark containing phloem is removed from a stem while xylem remains intact. Predict the initial effect on water supply above the ring and on sugar transport to roots. Explain a possible later effect on the whole plant.
challenges.answer: Initially xylem can still carry water upward because it remains continuous. Downward phloem transport of sugars across the ring is disrupted, so roots can lose their normal sugar supply. Root function can then decline, eventually compromising water uptake and the whole plant. The distinction depends on the specified tissues remaining intact or being removed.

topics.subject: life
topics.title: Ecology, nutrient cycles & biodiversity

notes.heading: How do food webs show energy flow?
notes.body: Arrows point from food to consumer, showing energy transfer. Producers form the first trophic level. Energy available usually decreases at higher levels because organisms respire and not all biomass is eaten or assimilated.

notes.heading: How do nutrient cycles differ from energy flow?
notes.body: Elements such as carbon and nitrogen are recycled. Decomposers break down organic material, returning nutrients to usable pools. Energy enters mainly as sunlight and leaves as heat.

notes.heading: What makes a relationship mutualistic?
notes.body: In mutualism both partners benefit. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria obtain organic nutrients from plants and supply biologically usable nitrogen compounds. Biodiversity includes genetic, species and ecosystem variation.

practice.question: In grass → locust → frog → snake, identify the producer and secondary consumer.
practice.answer: Grass is the producer. Locust is the primary consumer and frog is the secondary consumer. Snake is the tertiary consumer.

practice.question: Explain one effect of habitat fragmentation on biodiversity.
practice.answer: Fragments isolate populations and can reduce access to food, mates and migration routes. Smaller isolated populations are more vulnerable to local extinction, reducing biodiversity.

practice.question: Classify sunlight, soil temperature, fungi and grass as biotic or abiotic factors.
practice.answer: Sunlight and soil temperature are abiotic, non-living environmental factors. Fungi and grass are living organisms and are biotic factors.

practice.question: Explain why decomposers are important in a nutrient cycle.
practice.answer: They break down dead organisms and wastes, returning elements to environmental pools in forms that can be reused by producers. They recycle matter; they do not recycle energy back into sunlight.

practice.question: A food chain is algae → insect larvae → fish → heron. Identify the primary and tertiary consumers.
practice.answer: Insect larvae are primary consumers because they feed on the producer algae. Fish are secondary consumers and the heron is the tertiary consumer.

practice.question: Explain one benefit a plant and a nitrogen-fixing bacterium each receive in a mutualistic association.
practice.answer: The bacterium obtains organic nutrients supplied by the plant. The plant gains access to nitrogen compounds produced through bacterial nitrogen fixation. Both partners benefit.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: In a simplified ecosystem, producers store 20 000 kJ over a period. Assume 10% is transferred to each successive consumer level. Estimate energy available to primary, secondary and tertiary consumers. Explain two reasons real transfers do not follow an exact universal 10% rule.
challenges.answer: Estimated primary-consumer energy = 2 000 kJ; secondary = 200 kJ; tertiary = 20 kJ. Transfer efficiency varies with organisms and circumstances. Not all biomass is eaten or assimilated, and energy is used in respiration and dissipated as heat. The 10% figure is an assumption for this model, not a universal constant.

challenges.question: An isolated habitat loses its top predator and herbivore numbers initially rise. Propose a linked effect on vegetation and soil, then explain why the outcome cannot be predicted from a single food chain with certainty.
challenges.answer: More herbivores may increase grazing, reduce vegetation and expose soil, potentially increasing erosion. But alternative foods, other predators, disease, migration and plant regrowth can alter the outcome. A food web and environmental data are needed to assess competing interactions rather than treating one chain as a complete prediction.

topics.subject: life
topics.title: Evolution, climate & scientific essays

notes.heading: How do fossils provide evidence?
notes.body: Fossils record past organisms and change over time. Relative dating orders events or layers; numerical dating estimates ages. Interpret the actual scale and labels before comparing fossils.

notes.heading: How can climate change affect biodiversity?
notes.body: Changing temperatures, rainfall and habitats can shift ranges and disrupt feeding relationships. Some organisms disperse or adjust; others cannot keep pace. Distinguish evidence, uncertainty and unsupported claims.

notes.heading: How do you build a scientific argument?
notes.body: State a position, use specific source evidence and explain its relevance. Discuss counterarguments fairly and conclude in proportion to the evidence. Evaluate source reliability, methods and possible bias.

practice.question: Explain the difference between relative and numerical fossil dating.
practice.answer: Relative dating places fossils or rock layers in order from older to younger without assigning an exact age. Numerical dating estimates an age in years, often using radioactive isotope decay.

practice.question: Give one argument and one counterpoint for climate change causing species extinctions.
practice.answer: Argument: rapid habitat changes may exceed the ability of specialist species to move or adapt. Counterpoint: responses vary and some species can shift range, so evidence should be assessed by species and region rather than assuming all will go extinct.

practice.question: In an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary rock layers, fossil A is below fossil B. Which is generally older, and what assumption is necessary?
practice.answer: Fossil A is generally older under the principle of superposition. This assumes the layers have not been overturned or otherwise disturbed in a way that changes their original order.

practice.question: Why is a statement that all species will respond identically to climate change scientifically weak?
practice.answer: Species differ in tolerance, habitat needs, reproduction, dispersal and interactions with other organisms. Evidence about one species or region does not justify an identical prediction for every species.

practice.question: An essay source reports an observed decline in a species but does not measure its cause. Can that observation alone prove climate change caused the decline?
practice.answer: No. It documents a pattern but does not by itself establish causation. Alternative factors such as habitat loss, disease or sampling changes must be considered, and additional evidence is needed.

practice.question: Write a balanced concluding sentence for an essay on whether habitat change may cause extinctions.
practice.answer: Example: Habitat change can raise extinction risk, especially for specialists unable to disperse, but the outcome depends on its rate, the species involved and other pressures; conclusions should match the evidence in the sources.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: A source reports that 80% of a sample’s specialist species declined after a drought, compared with 30% of generalists. Build an evidence-based argument about vulnerability, give one alternative explanation, and state one limitation before generalising.
challenges.answer: The sample supports greater observed vulnerability among specialists in those conditions, potentially because narrow resource needs reduce flexibility. Alternative explanations include different habitat loss, disease exposure or sampling detectability between groups. Sample size, selection, location and duration must be examined; the percentages alone cannot establish a universal response or prove drought was the sole cause.

challenges.question: A fossil sequence shows a change in limb structure across several rock layers. Explain what this can support about change over time and two things it cannot establish without further evidence.
challenges.answer: If the layer sequence and fossil identification are reliable, it can support that organisms with different limb structures occurred at different times. It does not alone prove that one sampled fossil was the direct ancestor of another or identify the exact selective cause. Dating, broader anatomical evidence and other lines of evidence help evaluate those claims.

topics.subject: life
topics.title: Scientific investigations & practical skills

notes.heading: How do you distinguish variables?
notes.body: The independent variable is deliberately changed; the dependent variable is measured; controlled variables are held constant. A fair comparison changes one tested factor at a time.

notes.heading: What makes a useful hypothesis?
notes.body: State a testable predicted relationship, ideally with a biological reason. A conclusion must answer the aim using recorded evidence, rather than simply repeating the hypothesis.

notes.heading: How do you improve reliability and validity?
notes.body: Repeat measurements and calculate appropriate summaries to improve reliability. Control confounding factors, use suitable equipment and a comparison/control where appropriate to support validity.

topics.formula: Aim → hypothesis → variables → method → results → conclusion

practice.question: A learner tests how temperature affects amylase activity. Name the independent, dependent and two controlled variables.
practice.answer: Independent: temperature. Dependent: reaction rate or time to a defined endpoint. Controls: pH and enzyme concentration (also substrate concentration/volume where appropriate).

practice.question: Three repeat reaction times are 40 s, 42 s and 38 s. Calculate the mean and explain why repeats help.
practice.answer: Mean = (40 + 42 + 38)/3 = 40 s. Repeats help reveal random variation and anomalous results, making the estimate of typical performance more reliable.

practice.question: A learner tests how light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis. State the independent variable, one measurable dependent variable and two controls.
practice.answer: Independent: light intensity. Dependent: a suitable measure such as oxygen volume produced per minute. Controls could include temperature and carbon-dioxide availability, as well as plant species and size.

practice.question: Four repeated measurements are 12, 14, 13 and 13 units. Find the mean.
practice.answer: Mean = (12 + 14 + 13 + 13)/4 = 52/4 = 13 units. Repeats provide evidence of variation as well as a central estimate.

practice.question: Explain why repeating an experiment does not automatically remove systematic error.
practice.answer: A systematic error affects measurements in a consistent direction, such as a miscalibrated instrument. Repetition may reproduce the same bias; calibration or a corrected method is needed to address it.

practice.question: Write a testable hypothesis for an investigation of how temperature affects enzyme activity over a range below the enzyme’s optimum.
practice.answer: Example: Over the tested range below the optimum, increasing temperature will increase enzyme reaction rate because particles move more rapidly and form successful enzyme-substrate interactions more frequently.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: A learner counts oxygen bubbles from pondweed at distances of 10, 20 and 30 cm from a lamp. Rates are 24, 15 and 8 bubbles/min. Give a cautious conclusion, identify two confounders and propose two improvements.
challenges.answer: The observations are consistent with higher apparent photosynthetic output nearer the lamp, but distance itself is not a direct measurement of light intensity. Lamp heating and unequal bubble volumes can affect interpretation. Measure or control temperature, measure light intensity, collect oxygen volume instead of only bubble count, and repeat trials using comparable plant material.

challenges.question: A control group gives results 10, 11, 9 and a treated group 13, 30, 14 units. Find both means. Explain why automatically deleting 30 is poor practice and propose a defensible next step.
challenges.answer: Control mean = 30/3 = 10; treated mean = 57/3 = 19. The value 30 strongly affects the treated mean, but being unusual does not prove it is wrong. Check records, equipment and the pre-agreed exclusion rules, investigate a documented procedural error if present, and repeat measurements. Report the variation transparently rather than remove an inconvenient result without evidence.

topics.subject: sports
topics.title: Bones, muscles & movement

notes.heading: What does the skeleton do?
notes.body: The skeleton supports and protects the body, provides muscle attachment sites and acts as a lever system. Bones store minerals such as calcium and phosphorus; marrow produces blood cells.

notes.heading: How do antagonistic muscles work?
notes.body: Muscles generate pulling forces. For a particular movement the agonist produces the main action and the antagonist opposes or controls it. Their roles change when movement reverses.

notes.heading: What are contraction types?
notes.body: Isometric contraction develops tension with no overall muscle-length change. Concentric contraction shortens an active muscle; eccentric contraction lengthens an active muscle while controlling a load.

topics.formula: Muscle force → tendon → bone → joint movement

practice.question: During a controlled biceps curl upwards, identify the main agonist and contraction type.
practice.answer: The biceps brachii is a main elbow-flexion agonist and contracts concentrically as it shortens. The triceps acts as an antagonist.

practice.question: A learner holds a squat still. Name the contraction type and explain it.
practice.answer: The muscles maintaining the position act mainly isometrically. They produce tension without a visible change in overall muscle length or joint position.

practice.question: Name the three main bones of the arm and forearm, and identify which is in the upper arm.
practice.answer: The humerus is the upper-arm bone. The radius and ulna are the two forearm bones.

practice.question: During knee extension, identify the main agonist muscle group and an antagonistic group.
practice.answer: The quadriceps are the main knee-extension agonists. The hamstrings are an antagonistic knee-flexor group. Roles depend on the particular movement being analysed.

practice.question: A person slowly lowers a dumbbell from a flexed elbow. Describe the biceps contraction.
practice.answer: The biceps remains active while lengthening to control the lowering movement, so it contracts eccentrically rather than simply switching off.

practice.question: Give two protective functions of the skeleton, naming a structure and the organ it protects.
practice.answer: The skull protects the brain. The rib cage helps protect the heart and lungs. Other correct structure-organ examples can also be accepted.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: Analyse a slow squat in three phases: lowering, holding still, then rising. For the quadriceps, identify the main contraction type in each phase and explain why knee flexion during lowering does not mean the quadriceps are inactive.
challenges.answer: During controlled lowering the quadriceps are active while lengthening, so their action is eccentric. During a still hold they act mainly isometrically. During rising they shorten to extend the knees, so their action is concentric. Lowering requires control against the load; a muscle can actively produce tension while lengthening rather than switch off.

challenges.question: A report attributes improved lifting performance entirely to bigger muscles after a short training period. Give two other plausible contributors and explain why a single before-and-after performance measurement cannot separate them.
challenges.answer: Improved neural recruitment/coordination and better technique or familiarity with the test can increase measured performance. Motivation and measurement conditions can also matter. One before-and-after result combines these influences, so size measurements and suitable repeated, standardised tests are needed before attributing the gain to hypertrophy alone.

topics.title: Energy systems & exercise

notes.heading: How does the ATP-PC system work?
notes.body: Stored ATP and phosphocreatine provide very rapid energy for brief maximal efforts. Capacity is limited, and recovery between efforts helps replenish phosphocreatine stores.

notes.heading: How do glycolytic and aerobic systems differ?
notes.body: Anaerobic glycolysis supplies ATP rapidly from carbohydrate without direct oxygen use. Aerobic metabolism uses oxygen and can sustain ATP production from carbohydrate and fat over longer periods.

notes.heading: Do the systems switch on separately?
notes.body: All energy systems contribute together. Their relative contribution changes with intensity, duration and training. Use sporting examples to justify the dominant contribution rather than claiming exclusive use.

practice.question: Which energy system has a major role in a single maximal 5-second sprint, and why?
practice.answer: The ATP-PC system has a major role because it supplies ATP very quickly for a brief maximal effort. Other systems also contribute.

practice.question: Why is aerobic fitness useful in a match containing repeated sprints?
practice.answer: Aerobic metabolism supports activity between sprints and recovery, including phosphocreatine restoration. It helps the athlete sustain repeated efforts across the match.

practice.question: Compare the dominant energy contribution in a single maximal jump with that in a steady 30-minute run.
practice.answer: A single maximal jump relies heavily on the ATP-PC system because ATP is needed very rapidly for a brief effort. A steady 30-minute run has a major aerobic contribution. All systems overlap rather than operating exclusively.

practice.question: Why do short recovery periods between repeated maximal sprints affect the next sprint?
practice.answer: Phosphocreatine stores may not fully replenish, so the rapid ATP-PC contribution can be reduced. Other energy pathways contribute more, and fatigue may lower the athlete’s ability to repeat the same output.

practice.question: Name the molecule used directly to supply energy for muscle contraction and explain why energy systems must continually regenerate it.
practice.answer: ATP supplies energy directly through its breakdown. Stored ATP is limited, so metabolic pathways continually regenerate ATP from ADP to sustain muscle activity.

practice.question: Why is it inaccurate to say that aerobic metabolism begins only after anaerobic metabolism stops?
practice.answer: The pathways contribute simultaneously. Intensity and duration change their relative contributions; they are not separate switches that turn on only when another system stops.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: A match includes one 5-second maximal sprint, 20 seconds of low-intensity movement and another sprint. Explain why both ATP-PC and aerobic capacity matter and predict a possible effect if the recovery interval is shortened substantially.
challenges.answer: ATP-PC has a major role in rapid ATP supply during the brief maximal sprint. Aerobic metabolism supports the low-intensity period and recovery, including phosphocreatine restoration. Shorter recovery can leave less restoration before the next sprint and increase fatigue or the relative contribution of other pathways. All systems overlap throughout rather than switching exclusively.

challenges.question: An athlete completes a short maximal effort and a long steady effort. A commentator says the first produces “no aerobic energy” and the second “no anaerobic energy”. Critique both claims and relate the overlap to intensity and duration.
challenges.answer: Neither statement is accurate: energy pathways contribute together. Rapid ATP-PC and anaerobic glycolytic supply can have large relative roles at high intensity, while aerobic contribution becomes especially important in sustained work. The mix changes with demand, duration and training; calling a system dominant does not make all other contributions zero.

cards.back: Aerobic metabolism supports activity between sprints and recovery, including phosphocreatine restoration. It helps the athlete sustain repeated efforts across the match.

cards.front: Compare the dominant energy contribution in a single maximal jump with that in a steady 30-minute run.
cards.back: A single maximal jump relies heavily on the ATP-PC system because ATP is needed very rapidly for a brief effort. A steady 30-minute run has a major aerobic contribution. All systems overlap rather than operating exclusively.

cards.back: Phosphocreatine stores may not fully replenish, so the rapid ATP-PC contribution can be reduced. Other energy pathways contribute more, and fatigue may lower the athlete’s ability to repeat the same output.

cards.back: ATP supplies energy directly through its breakdown. Stored ATP is limited, so metabolic pathways continually regenerate ATP from ADP to sustain muscle activity.

cards.front: Why is it inaccurate to say that aerobic metabolism begins only after anaerobic metabolism stops?
cards.back: The pathways contribute simultaneously. Intensity and duration change their relative contributions; they are not separate switches that turn on only when another system stops.

cards.front: A match includes one 5-second maximal sprint, 20 seconds of low-intensity movement and another sprint. Explain why both ATP-PC and aerobic capacity matter and predict a possible effect if the recovery interval is shortened substantially.

cards.front: An athlete completes a short maximal effort and a long steady effort. A commentator says the first produces “no aerobic energy” and the second “no anaerobic energy”. Critique both claims and relate the overlap to intensity and duration.

cards.front: Why does phosphocreatine need recovery time?
cards.back: Its limited stores must be replenished after use; aerobic processes support this recovery.

cards.front: Which energy supply molecule is used directly for muscle contraction?
cards.back: ATP.

cards.front: Why can the dominant system differ within one sport?
cards.back: Intensity and duration vary between actions and recovery periods.

cards.front: Does lactate formation by itself explain all exercise fatigue?
cards.back: No. Fatigue has multiple interacting physiological causes.

topics.subject: sports
topics.title: Levers & anatomical planes

notes.heading: What are the parts of a lever?
notes.body: A lever is a rigid structure rotating around a fulcrum. Effort is the applied force and load is the resistance. The effort and load arms are perpendicular moment-arm distances from the pivot to force lines.

notes.heading: How are lever classes organised?
notes.body: First class has the fulcrum in the middle; second class has the load in the middle; third class has effort in the middle. Third-class levers often favour speed and range over force advantage.

notes.heading: Which movements occur in each plane?
notes.body: Sagittal: flexion and extension. Frontal: abduction and adduction. Transverse: rotation. Name the joint and movement, and distinguish the movement plane from the axis perpendicular to it.

practice.question: In a lever, effort lies between the fulcrum and the load. Name the class and give a body example.
practice.answer: It is a third-class lever. In elbow flexion, the elbow is the fulcrum, the biceps applies effort near the elbow and the load is farther along the forearm/hand.

practice.question: A 30 N force acts at a perpendicular distance of 0.2 m from a pivot. Find the torque.
practice.answer: Torque = 30 × 0.2 = 6 N·m. The perpendicular distance to the force line, rather than any arbitrary bone length, must be used.

practice.question: In a lever, the load is between the fulcrum and effort. Identify the class and a human-body example.
practice.answer: This is a second-class lever. Rising onto the toes is a common example: the ball of the foot is the fulcrum, body weight is the load, and calf-muscle force through the Achilles tendon supplies effort.

practice.question: A force of 80 N acts with a perpendicular moment arm of 0.15 m. Calculate the torque.
practice.answer: Torque = force × perpendicular moment arm = 80 × 0.15 = 12 N·m.

practice.question: Identify the main anatomical plane of elbow flexion, shoulder abduction and trunk rotation.
practice.answer: Elbow flexion occurs in the sagittal plane; shoulder abduction in the frontal plane; trunk rotation in the transverse plane.

practice.question: For a balanced lever, a 40 N load acts 0.3 m from the pivot. What effort is required with a perpendicular moment arm of 0.6 m?
practice.answer: Balance torques: effort × 0.6 = 40 × 0.3 = 12 N·m. Effort = 12/0.6 = 20 N, assuming these are the only relevant torques.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: A forearm is held horizontal. Ignore forearm weight. A 40 N load acts 0.30 m from the elbow, while the biceps has a perpendicular moment arm of 0.04 m. Find the required biceps force, identify the lever class and explain its force disadvantage.
challenges.answer: Balance torques: F × 0.04 = 40 × 0.30 = 12 N·m, so F = 300 N. The effort lies between the elbow fulcrum and hand load, making it a third-class lever. The short effort arm means a force much larger than the load is needed; this arrangement can favour speed and range of movement.

challenges.question: A 60 N effort acts with perpendicular arm 0.20 m against a 40 N load. Find the load arm required for balance. Explain what happens to the required effort if its moment arm is halved while the load torque stays fixed.
challenges.answer: Effort torque = 60 × 0.20 = 12 N·m. Balance requires 40d = 12, giving d = 0.30 m. If the effort arm halves, the effort must double to 120 N to provide the same torque, assuming other forces remain unchanged.

topics.subject: sports
topics.title: Nutrition & exercise fuel

notes.heading: What do macronutrients supply?
notes.body: Carbohydrate and protein each supply about 4 kcal/g; fat supplies about 9 kcal/g. Carbohydrate is an important exercise fuel; protein supports growth and repair; fat also supports membranes, insulation and vitamin absorption.

notes.heading: What does glycaemic index compare?
notes.body: GI compares the blood-glucose response to equal amounts of available carbohydrate from different foods. It is affected by food processing and meal context. A carbohydrate-free food is not meaningfully assigned a low GI.

notes.heading: How should you evaluate a diet claim?
notes.body: Ask what evidence supports it, whether the study population matches the claim and whether a source is selling something. School questions about a diet are an opportunity to evaluate evidence, not a personal meal prescription.

topics.formula: Energy ≈ 4 × carbohydrate g + 4 × protein g + 9 × fat g

practice.question: A snack contains 20 g carbohydrate, 5 g protein and 4 g fat. Estimate energy in kcal.
Why is it misleading to describe a carbohydrate-free food as low GI?
practice.answer: GI is measured using a portion containing a standard amount of available carbohydrate. A food with essentially none cannot be compared on that basis, so its GI is generally not applicable.

practice.question: Estimate the energy in a food portion containing 30 g carbohydrate, 10 g protein and 6 g fat. Use 4, 4 and 9 kcal/g respectively.
Distinguish a small calorie from a kilocalorie and convert 250 kcal to small calories.
practice.answer: A kilocalorie equals 1 000 small calories. Therefore 250 kcal = 250 000 cal. Food energy labelled Calories commonly refers to kilocalories.

practice.question: State two functions of dietary fat other than supplying energy.
practice.answer: Fat provides components used in cell membranes and supports absorption of fat-soluble vitamins. It also contributes to insulation and cushioning. These are general biological roles, not a personal diet prescription.

practice.question: A sports-diet article uses one athlete’s success as proof that its diet works for everyone. Give two reasons to question the claim.
practice.answer: A single anecdote cannot establish a general effect, and other influences such as training, genetics and total energy intake may explain the success. A stronger claim needs suitable comparative evidence from relevant populations.

topics.tip: Use these as exam concepts. One nutritional calorie (kcal) is 1 000 small calories; the supplied memo uses the word calorie loosely.

challenges.question: Snack A has 25 g carbohydrate, 8 g protein and 10 g fat; B has 35 g carbohydrate, 8 g protein and 4 g fat. Use 4, 4 and 9 kcal/g. Compare total energy and explain why equal or similar energy does not make their nutritional effects identical.
challenges.answer: A supplies 25(4) + 8(4) + 10(9) = 222 kcal. B supplies 35(4) + 8(4) + 4(9) = 208 kcal. A provides 14 kcal more, but the macronutrient amounts differ. Fibre, food form, micronutrients, digestion and activity context also matter, so one energy total cannot establish identical nutritional effects or a personal best choice.

challenges.question: A sports article claims a diet caused faster race times because 8 of 10 volunteers improved after adopting it. Evaluate the claim and describe a stronger comparison that would help distinguish diet from training effects.
challenges.answer: Improvement in 8/10 is descriptive evidence, not proof of cause. Training changes, expectation, familiarity, participant selection and normal variation could contribute. A stronger design would use an appropriate comparison group, standardised testing and recorded training, suitable allocation, repeated outcomes and clear reporting. The claim should stay within what the study can support, rather than become advice for every athlete.

topics.subject: sports
topics.title: Heart, lungs & aerobic fitness

notes.heading: What is cardiac output?
notes.body: Cardiac output is the volume pumped by a ventricle per minute. It equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. Keep mL and L consistent when calculating.

notes.heading: What is VO₂ max?
notes.body: VO₂ max is the maximum rate of oxygen consumption during intense exercise, often expressed as mL/kg/min. It reflects the integrated ability to deliver and use oxygen, not simply lung size.

notes.heading: How does training affect endurance?
notes.body: Endurance training can increase stroke volume, capillary density and mitochondrial capacity, and lower resting heart rate. Adaptations depend on the training programme and the individual.

topics.formula: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume

practice.question: Heart rate is 150 beats/min and stroke volume is 120 mL/beat. Find cardiac output in L/min.
practice.answer: Q = 150 × 120 = 18 000 mL/min. Divide by 1 000: Q = 18 L/min.

practice.question: Why do thin alveolar walls and many surrounding capillaries support gas exchange?
practice.answer: Thin walls reduce diffusion distance. The capillary network supplies a large exchange area and helps maintain oxygen and carbon-dioxide concentration gradients.

practice.question: An athlete has cardiac output 24 L/min and heart rate 160 beats/min. Calculate stroke volume in mL/beat.
practice.answer: Stroke volume = cardiac output/heart rate = 24/160 = 0.15 L/beat. Multiply by 1 000: 150 mL/beat.

practice.question: At rest, heart rate is 60 beats/min and stroke volume 80 mL/beat. Calculate cardiac output in L/min.
practice.answer: Q = HR × SV = 60 × 80 = 4 800 mL/min = 4.8 L/min.

practice.question: Explain why oxygen transport depends on both the cardiovascular and respiratory systems.
practice.answer: The respiratory system ventilates the lungs and provides gas-exchange surfaces. The cardiovascular system carries oxygen in blood to working tissues. Good gas exchange alone cannot deliver oxygen without circulation.

practice.question: Distinguish an increase in breathing rate during exercise from an increase in mitochondrial capacity after training.
practice.answer: A rise in breathing rate during a bout of exercise is an acute response. Greater mitochondrial capacity developed through repeated appropriate training is a chronic adaptation that can support aerobic ATP production.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: Two athletes each have cardiac output 20 L/min at a test stage. A’s heart rate is 160 beats/min and B’s is 125. Find their stroke volumes and explain why this alone does not prove which has the higher VO₂ max.
challenges.answer: A: SV = 20/160 = 0.125 L/beat = 125 mL/beat. B: SV = 20/125 = 0.160 L/beat = 160 mL/beat. VO₂ max depends on more than stroke volume at one test stage, including oxygen transport and extraction, and the stage may not be maximal. The numbers alone cannot rank their maximum aerobic capacity.

challenges.question: After months of endurance training, an athlete’s resting heart rate falls from 72 to 60 beats/min while resting cardiac output stays 4.8 L/min. Calculate stroke volume before and after, then link the change to the maintained output.
challenges.answer: Before: SV = 4.8/72 = 0.0667 L/beat ≈ 66.7 mL/beat. After: SV = 4.8/60 = 0.080 L/beat = 80 mL/beat. A larger volume per beat compensates for fewer beats per minute, preserving the stated resting output. This is consistent with an endurance adaptation under the given assumptions.

topics.subject: sports
topics.title: Arousal, psychology & motor skills

notes.heading: What is the inverted-U model?
notes.body: Performance may improve as arousal rises toward an optimum and then fall as arousal becomes excessive. The optimum varies with the task, skill level and individual; it is a model rather than a universal law.

notes.heading: How do skill demands differ?
notes.body: Fine skills require precise small-muscle control; gross skills use larger muscle groups. Complex tasks often need greater attentional control. Do not assume every athlete has the same optimum arousal.

notes.heading: How can an athlete regulate arousal?
notes.body: Breathing routines, imagery and attention cues can help manage arousal. Match a strategy to the athlete and task, and explain how it could support concentration or readiness.

topics.formula: Low arousal → optimum zone → excessive arousal

practice.question: Use the inverted-U model to explain why too much arousal can hurt a precision task.
practice.answer: Arousal above the athlete’s optimum can increase tension and disrupt attention and fine control. This may reduce accuracy in a precision task such as putting.

practice.question: Give two ways an athlete could reduce excessive pre-match arousal.
practice.answer: Controlled breathing can help regulate physiological activation. A familiar attention routine or calming imagery can redirect focus toward useful task cues.

practice.question: Use the inverted-U model to explain why an athlete who is too relaxed might perform poorly.
practice.answer: Arousal below the athlete’s optimum may reduce alertness, readiness or effort. An appropriate increase could improve performance toward the optimum, but excessive arousal may then impair it.

practice.question: Classify precision dart throwing and a powerful whole-body jump as mainly fine or gross motor skills.
practice.answer: Precision dart throwing depends strongly on fine motor control and accuracy. A powerful jump depends mainly on gross motor coordination and large muscle groups, although both tasks involve several control processes.

practice.question: Two athletes perform the same event but prefer different pre-competition routines. Does the inverted-U model require them to have the same optimal arousal?
practice.answer: No. Optimal arousal can depend on the individual, experience and task demands. The model does not establish one identical level or routine for every athlete.

practice.question: Explain how a short attention cue could help an athlete who is distracted by worries during a skill.
practice.answer: A relevant cue, such as focusing on the target or a movement step, can redirect attention toward controllable task information. The explanation should connect the cue to the specific skill rather than assume all distraction will vanish.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: A precision-task athlete scores 60, 82 and 65 under low, moderate and high arousal conditions. Explain how these observations fit an inverted-U model, then give two reasons they do not establish a universal optimal level.
challenges.answer: The middle condition gives the highest observed performance, consistent with improvement toward an optimum and impairment beyond it. But there are only three conditions and results may be affected by practice, fatigue or measurement error. Athletes and tasks differ, so these data cannot locate one exact optimum or generalise it to every person or sport.

challenges.question: One athlete prepares for a maximal jump and another for a precision putt. Propose how their arousal strategies might differ, justify with task demands and explain why the proposal should still be individualised.
challenges.answer: The jumper may benefit from a routine increasing readiness and forceful effort, while the putter may use breathing or attention cues to limit distracting tension and support precise control. Task demands justify the different emphasis, but skill, preference and prior responses vary. Evaluate the actual athlete rather than assume one routine or arousal level always works.

topics.title: Training adaptations & evidence-based essays

notes.heading: How do training principles guide progress?
notes.body: Specificity means adaptations match the training demand. Progressive overload gradually increases that demand. Recovery allows adaptation; excessive load without recovery can impair performance.

notes.heading: Which adaptations are relevant?
notes.body: Resistance training can increase strength and muscle size; endurance training can increase aerobic capacity and fatigue resistance. Separate immediate exercise responses from adaptations developed over weeks or months.

notes.heading: How do you evaluate performance limits?
notes.body: Use evidence about physiology, training, technology and participation. Consider both biological constraints and changes that allow progress. Distinguish fair technological improvements from prohibited practices without assuming a source is neutral.

practice.question: Distinguish an acute response to running from a long-term endurance adaptation.
practice.answer: A raised heart rate during a run is an acute response. An increased stroke volume after months of appropriate endurance training is a chronic adaptation.

practice.question: Give one supported argument on each side of whether athletic records can continue improving.
practice.answer: For improvement: better training methods, technology and wider participation can improve performance. For limits: human physiology places constraints on oxygen delivery, force production and recovery. A conclusion should weigh the evidence for the specific sport.

practice.question: Explain progressive overload using a strength-training example without prescribing a personal programme.
practice.answer: Progressive overload means gradually increasing the training demand as adaptation occurs. For example, a suitable programme may progressively raise resistance or work volume, while allowing recovery and maintaining appropriate technique.

practice.question: Why does a training programme need specificity?
practice.answer: The body adapts to the demands imposed. Training should therefore reflect relevant movements, muscle groups and energy demands; adaptations from one type of training do not transfer equally to every sport.

practice.question: Distinguish a response from an adaptation using two cardiovascular examples.
practice.answer: An increased heart rate during one exercise session is a response. A lower resting heart rate associated with sustained endurance training can be an adaptation. The timescale and repeated stimulus distinguish them.

practice.question: An essay source says new equipment caused a sporting record. What additional evidence would help assess that claim?
practice.answer: Compare performance with and without the equipment under similar conditions, considering training, athlete ability, rules and measurement methods. A record occurring after a new design appeared is not enough by itself to prove the equipment caused it.

challenges.question: A runner’s time improves after a programme that changes training load, footwear and sleep habits together. Construct a cautious conclusion, identify the attribution problem and propose a way to improve the evidence.
challenges.answer: The combined programme is associated with an improvement in this runner, but the design cannot isolate training load from footwear, sleep or other influences. Use standardised repeated tests and appropriate comparison conditions, changing or measuring the candidate influences systematically. The conclusion should not claim one cause without evidence separating it from the alternatives.

challenges.question: An essay argues that a new record proves human performance has no limits. Build a response using one argument for further improvement, one biological constraint and a reason the conclusion is too strong.
challenges.answer: Better training, technology or wider participation can enable further records. However, oxygen delivery, force production, recovery and other biological processes impose constraints. One new record only shows that the previous best was surpassed; it does not prove unlimited improvement. A balanced conclusion should be specific to the sport, evidence and timescale.

cards.front: How do training principles guide progress?
cards.back: Specificity means adaptations match the training demand. Progressive overload gradually increases that demand. Recovery allows adaptation; excessive load without recovery can impair performance.
